Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We had certainly given Luqman wisdom, [saying], "Be grateful to God. And whoever is grateful is grateful only for [the benefit of] himself; and whoever disbelieves - indeed, God is Free of need and Praiseworthy."﴾

This is an allusion to a meaning, namely that following the Prophet, peace be upon him, is obligatory even in matters whose meaning is not understood, as a demonstration of devotion (ta'abbud). So how much more so for matters that are not specific to prophethood, but whose meaning is grasped by the intellect. What the Prophet, peace be upon him, brought is apprehended through wisdom. He mentioned the account of Luqman and that he grasped it through wisdom. His saying: ﴿And We had certainly given Luqman wisdom﴾ is an expression for the success of acting in accordance with knowledge. So everyone who is granted success in acting in accordance with knowledge has been granted wisdom. If we wish to define it by what includes the wisdom of God, exalted is He, we say: wisdom is the occurrence of action in conformity with what is known.

What indicates what we have mentioned is that whoever learns something without knowing its benefits and harms is not called wise; rather, he is merely a fool. Do you not see that whoever throws himself from a high place, falls on a spot where the ground gives way beneath him, and he discovers a treasure and is unharmed, is not called wise? Even if his act produced a benefit free of harm, it is because he did not know it beforehand. And whoever knows that throwing himself there will destroy his soul, yet throws himself from that place and his limbs are broken, is not called wise, even though he knew what would result from his act.

So God explained the granting of wisdom by His saying: ﴿that be grateful to God﴾. This is indeed so, because among what is said is that action conforms to knowledge: when a person knows two matters, one of which is more important than the other, if he occupies himself with the more important, his action conforms to his knowledge and is wisdom. If he neglects the more important, his action contradicts his knowledge and is not wisdom in any respect. But the gratitude to God is the most important of things, so wisdom first requires it.

Then God, exalted is He, clarified that by gratitude only the grateful person benefits, through His saying: ﴿And whoever is grateful is grateful only for [the benefit of] himself﴾. And He clarified that by ingratitude no one other than the disbeliever is harmed, through His saying: ﴿and whoever disbelieves - indeed, God is Free of need and Praiseworthy﴾. That is, God does not need gratitude so that He would be harmed by the ingratitude of the disbeliever. He is praiseworthy in Himself, whether people thank Him or not.

There are issues and subtleties in the verse.

The answer: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿that be grateful to God﴾ is a command of creation (amr takwin), meaning: We granted him wisdom by making him among the grateful. Although the conditional structure makes the past and the future have one meaning, as when someone says: "Whoever enters my house is free," and "Whoever enters my house is free," we say that there is an allusion here to a meaning and a guidance to a matter: gratitude should be repeated at every time, because the blessing is repeated. Also, the gratitude of the grateful person never occurs in its completeness; rather, there is always something lacking, which the grateful person wishes to bring into existence, as he said: ﴿My Lord, enable me to be grateful for Your favor﴾ [al-Naml: 19], and as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if you should count the favor of God, you could not enumerate it﴾ [Ibrahim: 34]. We say: there, the mention was for warning (tarhib), due to His saying earlier: ﴿So set your face toward the upright religion before there comes from God a Day which no one can avert. His saying: ﴿And whoever does righteousness﴾ confirms what we mentioned first. Since what is mentioned in Surah al-Rum comes after the Day which cannot be averted, the deeds have already preceded, so He said in the past form: ﴿And whoever does﴾. Here, since what is mentioned is at the beginning, He said: ﴿And whoever is grateful﴾ in the imperfect form. His saying: ﴿and whoever disbelieves - indeed, God is Free of need﴾ means: free of the praise of those who praise Him, praiseworthy in His essence without their praise. The one who praises only has his rank raised by being one who praises God, exalted is He.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 31, verses 13–14:

Then God Most High said: ﴿And when Luqman said to his son, while he was advising him, "O my son, do not associate anything with God. Indeed, association [with God] is a tremendous wrong."﴾

This is a conjunction with the meaning of what preceded it. Its implied sense is: "We gave Luqman wisdom when We made him grateful in himself, and when We made him an advisor to others." This is because the elevation of a human being's rank lies in being perfect in himself and perfecting others. So His saying ﴿that give thanks﴾ is an indication of perfection, and His saying ﴿And when Luqman said to his son, while he was advising him﴾ is an indication of completing others. In this there is a subtle point: God mentioned Luqman and praised his effort in that he guided his son, so that from it there might be known the virtue of the Prophet (ﷺ), who guided strangers and relatives. For guiding one's own child is a customary matter, whereas bearing hardship in teaching distant people is not. Then, in his admonition, he began with the most important matter, which is prohibition of associating partners with God, and said: ﴿Indeed, association [with God] is a tremendous wrong.﴾ As for it being a wrong, it is because it is placing the noble, honored soul, which God Most High has honored in His saying ﴿And We have certainly honored the children of Adam﴾ [al-Isra: 70], in the worship of what is base. Or it is because it is placing worship in other than its proper place, and that place is other than the face of God and His way. As for it being tremendous, it is because it has been placed in a position that is not its position, and it cannot be its position. This is because one who takes the wealth of Zayd and gives it to Amr is committing a wrong insofar as he has placed Zayd's wealth in Amr's possession; but it is permissible that this be Amr's property, or that it become his property through a prior sale or a subsequent transfer of ownership. As for association, it is placing divinity (ma'budiyyah) in other than God Most High, and it is not permissible that anyone other than Him be worshipped at all.

His saying ﴿Allah will bring it forth﴾ is more eloquent than the statement of one who says "Allah knows it," because one to whom a thing becomes manifest but who cannot make it manifest to others is in a state of knowledge lower than one to whom a thing becomes manifest and who makes it manifest to others. So His saying ﴿Allah will bring it forth﴾ means Allah will make it manifest for the purpose of bearing witness. His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah is Subtle﴾ means: of pervasive power; ﴿Acquainted﴾ means: knowing the inner realities of affairs.

Then His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if they strive with you to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge, do not obey them, but accompany them in this world with kindness. And follow the way of those who turn back to Me in repentance. Then to Me will be your return, and I will inform you about what you used to do.﴾ ﴿O my son, indeed it, if it should be the weight of a mustard seed and should be within a rock or in the heavens or on the earth, Allah will bring it forth. Indeed, Allah is Subtle and Acquainted.﴾

It means that serving them is obligatory and obeying them is binding, so long as it does not involve abandoning the obedience of Allah.

As for when it leads to that, then do not obey them. We have already mentioned the explanation of this verse in Surat al-Ankabut. He said here: ﴿And follow the way of those who turn back to Me﴾, meaning: accompany them with your body, for their right over your body is due, and follow the way of the Prophet, peace be upon him, with your intellect, for he is the one who nurtures your intellect, just as the father nurtures your body.

He, exalted is He, said: ﴿O my son, indeed it, if it should be the weight of a mustard seed and should be within a rock or in the heavens or on the earth, Allah will bring it forth. Indeed, Allah is Subtle and Acquainted.﴾

When He said: ﴿Then I will inform you about what you used to do﴾, it occurred to his son that what one does in secret is hidden, so he said: ﴿O my son, indeed it﴾, that is, the good deed and the bad deed, if it is in smallness like a mustard seed, and it is, with that smallness, in a secure place like a rock, it is not hidden from Allah. And in this there are issues:

The first issue: His saying ﴿fa-takun﴾ with the fa' (fa', the particle of sequence) is to convey conjunction, meaning: if it is small, and with its smallness it is hidden in a secure place like a rock, it is not hidden from Allah; for the fa' indicates connection through immediate succession.

The second issue: If it is said that the rock must be either in the heavens or in the earth, what is the benefit of mentioning it? Moreover, if a speaker said: "This is a man, or a woman, or the son of 'Amr," this statement would not be correct, because the son of 'Amr is included in one of the two divisions. How then is this understood? We say the answer to it is from several aspects.

The first of them: what some of the exegetes have said, namely that the rock intended is a rock upon which there is a bull, and it is neither in the earth nor in the sky.

The second: what al-Zamakhshari said, namely that there is an ellipsis in it, its estimate being: "then it will be in a rock, or in another place, in the heavens or in the earth."

The third: we say that mentioning the particular before the general in such a division is permissible, whereas mentioning the general before the particular is not permissible.

As for the second: since you have shown that whoever says this is in the house of Zayd, or elsewhere, or in the house of 'Amr, is not correct, because the house of 'Amr is included in his saying "or elsewhere." As for the first: the saying of the speaker, "This is in the house of Zayd, or in the house of 'Amr, or elsewhere," is correct and not objectionable; likewise here he mentioned the more specific first. Or we say: the hiddenness of a thing occurs through several means: among them that it be in extreme smallness, among them that it be far away, among them that it be in darkness, and among them that it be behind a veil. If all these conditions are absent, namely that it be large, near, in light, and without a veil, then it is not hidden from the one who is worshipped. Thus Allah affirmed seeing and knowledge together with the absence of these conditions.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 31, verse 17:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O my dear son, establish the prayer, enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong, and be patient over what befalls you. Indeed, that is among the matters requiring resolve.﴾

When he (Luqman) forbade him from associating partners with God and warned him by God's knowledge and power, he commanded him with what is incumbent upon him of monotheism (tawhid), which is the prayer (salat), and it is worship directed to the face of God, sincerely. By this it is known that the prayer existed in all the religious communities (milal), although its form differed.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And enjoin what is right, and forbid what is wrong﴾, meaning: when you have perfected yourself in the worship of God, then perfect others, for the occupation of the prophets and their heirs among the scholars ('ulama') is that they perfect themselves and perfect others. If someone says: how did he (Luqman) give precedence in his counsel to his son to enjoining what is right over forbidding what is wrong, whereas earlier he gave precedence to forbidding what is wrong over enjoining what is right, for he first said ﴿O my dear son, do not associate partners﴾ and then said ﴿O my dear son, establish the prayer﴾? We say: he knew of his son that he acknowledged the existence of God, so he did not command him with this right (ma'ruf) and forbid him from the wrong (munkar) that follows from this right. For one who associates partners with God does not, in belief, deny God, although it is necessary for him to deny Him by proof. So every right (ma'ruf) has a corresponding wrong (munkar). The right in the knowledge of God is believing in His existence, and the wrong is believing in the existence of something other along with Him. So he did not command him with that right, since it had already been achieved, and he forbade him from the wrong, because it has been reported in the tafsir that his son was a polytheist, so he admonished him and did not cease admonishing him until he embraced Islam. As for here, he commanded in an absolute manner, and the right takes precedence over the wrong.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And be patient over what befalls you﴾, meaning: whoever enjoins what is right and forbids what is wrong will be harmed, so he commanded him to be patient over it. His saying: ﴿Indeed, that is among the matters requiring resolve﴾ means: among the obligatory matters that are resolved upon, i.e., firmly decided. The verbal noun (masdar) here carries the sense of the passive participle (maf'ul), as when you say: "My eating during the day is a loaf of bread," meaning: "my food."

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And do not turn your cheek away from people, and do not walk on the earth exultantly. Indeed, God does not love every arrogant boaster.﴾

When He commanded him to be perfect in himself and to perfect others, and he would fear after these two things two matters: one of them is arrogance toward others because of his being one who perfects them, and the second is strutting in oneself because of his being perfect in himself. So He said: ﴿And do not turn your cheek away from people﴾ out of arrogance, ﴿and do not walk on the earth exultantly﴾ strutting. ﴿Indeed, God does not love every arrogant boaster﴾ meaning one who has conceit (khuyala', i.e., self-admiration), who shows people the greatness of his own self, which is arrogance; ﴿boaster﴾ meaning one who is proud of himself, who sees greatness in himself in his own eyes. In the verse there is a subtle point, namely that God, exalted is He, placed perfection (al-kamal, being complete oneself) before perfecting others (al-takmil), when He said ﴿Establish the prayer﴾ and then said ﴿and enjoin what is right﴾. In the prohibition, He placed what produces perfecting others before what produces perfection in oneself, when He said ﴿do not turn your cheek away﴾ and then said ﴿do not walk on the earth exultantly﴾. This is because on the affirmative side, one who is not perfect cannot become one who perfects others, so He placed perfection first. On the negative side, one who is arrogant toward others is also strutting; for he is not arrogant toward others except when he believes that he is in some respect greater than them. As for one who struts in himself, he is not arrogant, and he imagines that he is humble toward people. So He placed the negation of arrogance before the negation of strutting; for if He had negated strutting, it would necessarily have entailed the negation of arrogance, and so there would be no need to forbid it separately. An example of this: it is not permissible to say "Do not break your fast and do not eat," because one who does not break his fast does not eat; but it is permissible to say "Do not eat and do not break your fast," because one who does not eat may break his fast by other than eating. And a speaker may say that such a statement is explanatory, so that he says "Do not break your fast and do not eat," meaning do not break your fast by eating, and it is not two prohibitions but one.

When he said, ﴿And do not walk on the earth exultantly﴾, the absence of that may come in its opposite, which is the one who goes to the furthest extreme of deviation: the gait of the one who feigns death, who shows himself as weak out of asceticism. So he said, ﴿And be moderate in your walking﴾, meaning: be a middle course between the two blameworthy extremes. There are several questions concerning this verse.

**The first question:** Is there any connection between the command to lower one's voice and the command to be moderate in walking? We say: yes, whether we know it or not. The words of God contain benefits that no limit can contain, no count can reach, and no one knows. The apparent points are these:

The first: Since man is noble, his aims are noble, so their failure is a serious matter. God therefore enabled man to attain them by walking. If he cannot reach his goal, he calls out to what he seeks so that it stops for him, or he walks to it. If he cannot make his speech reach it, [he raises his voice]. Some animals share with man the attainment of their desires through sound, just as sheep call for their young, the cow for her calf, and the she-camel for her foal, with bleating, lowing and groaning. But they do not extend this to other things, whereas man distinguishes one thing from another. So when walking and voice both lead to a single goal, God guided him to one of them and guided him to the other as well.

The second: Man has three things. One is action by the limbs, in which animals share with him, for it is movement and stillness. Another is speech by the tongue, in which no other shares with him. The third is resolve in the heart, which no one knows of except God. He has pointed to this in His words: ﴿Indeed, if it is the weight of a mustard seed﴾, meaning: set right your inner self, for God is Aware. The two remaining matters were mentioned, so He said: ﴿And be moderate in your walking and lower your voice﴾, as an indication of moderation in deeds and in words.

The third: Luqman wished to guide his son to rectitude in the human qualities, in the qualities belonging to the angel, which is higher in rank than man, and in the qualities belonging to the animal, which is lower in rank than man. So his words, ﴿And enjoin what is good and forbid what is evil﴾, point to the noble qualities specific to man, for an angel does not command another angel to do anything, nor forbid him from anything. His words, ﴿And do not turn your cheek away from people, nor walk on the earth exultantly﴾, which indicate the avoidance of arrogance and strutting, point to the noble qualities that are the attributes of the angels, for avoiding arrogance and strutting is their attribute. His words, ﴿And be moderate in your walking and lower your voice﴾, point to the noble qualities that are the attributes of animals. Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, the most hateful of voices is the braying of donkeys﴾. On this there are several questions:

**The first question:** Why did He mention what prevents raising the voice, but not what prevents hastening the walk? We say: As for our view that walking and voice both convey one to a desired person, if one reaches him by walking to him, well and good; otherwise one stops him by calling out. We say that raising the voice harms the listener and strikes the ear canal forcefully, and may perhaps tear the membrane inside the ear. As for speed in walking, it does not harm, or if it does, it harms only those in its path, while the voice reaches those on the right and on the left. Also, walking harms the instrument of walking, while the voice harms the instrument of hearing, and the instrument of hearing is at the gate of the heart, for speech passes from hearing to the heart, which is not the case with walking. And as for our view that the reference by the thing and the voice is to deeds and words: the ugliness of speech is uglier than the ugliness of deed, and its goodness is better, because the tongue is the interpreter of the heart, and reasoning confirms the claim.

**The second question:** How is it understood that it is the most hateful, when the grinding of a saw with a file and the rubbing of copper with iron are more repulsive? We answer this in two ways:

One: What is meant is that the most hateful of the voices of animals is the voice of donkeys, so what you mentioned does not refute it. What you mentioned is, for the most part, for a benefit and for construction, so it is not considered hateful. This is unlike the voice of donkeys, and this is the second answer.

**The third question:** *Ankar* is the elative form (*af'al al-tafdil*). From which pattern is it? We say: It may be from the pattern of *atwa'a lahu min bananihi*, meaning the most obedient of his fingertips, for *af'al* does not come from *maf'al*, nor from *maf'ul*, nor from the pattern of defects, except in anomalous cases, such as their saying *atwa'u min kadhā* for preference over the one who obeys, and *ashghalu min dhāti al-nihyayn* for preference over the one who is busy, and *ahmaqu min fulān* from the pattern of defects. On this basis it is in the pattern of *af'ala* like *ashghala* in the pattern of *maf'ul*, so it is for preference over the one who is *munkar*. Or we say: it is from the pattern of *ashghala*, taken from *nakira al-shay'* (he found the thing strange), so he is *munkar* and this is *ankar* than him. On this basis it has a subtle meaning: every animal's voice may be understood to indicate that it cries out from heaviness or fatigue, like the camel, or otherwise. But the donkey, if it dies under its load, does not cry out; if it is slaughtered, it does not cry out; and at times when there is no need, it brays and hee-haws. So its voice is *mankur* (repugnant). It may also be said that it derives from *nakir*, like *ajdar* from *jadir*.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 31, verse 20:

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Do you not see that God has subjected to you whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and has completed His favours upon you, outward and inward? Yet among the people is one who disputes about God without knowledge, without guidance, and without an illuminating Book.﴾

When He had argued for the oneness (tawhid) of God through His words, ﴿He created the heavens without pillars [that you can see]﴾ [Luqman: 10], and had shown through the account of Luqman that knowing this is not restricted to prophethood but is in accordance with wisdom (hikmah), and that what the Prophet (peace be upon him) brought of monotheism, prayer and noble character is all profound wisdom, and that if it were purely devotional (ta'abbud mahd) its acceptance would be obligatory, quite apart from its being in accordance with wisdom, He argued for oneness through favour. This is because we have explained repeatedly that a king is served for his greatness even if he does not bestow favours, and is also served for his favours. So when He had shown that He is the one worthy of worship for His greatness, through creating the heavens without pillars and casting the firm mountains onto the earth, and mentioned some of the favours in His words ﴿And We sent down water from the sky﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 18], He then mentioned the favours in general, saying ﴿He subjected to you whatever is in the heavens﴾, meaning He subjected to you, for your sake, whatever is in the heavens. The sun, the moon and the stars are subjected by God's command, and in them are benefits for His servants. He subjected what is on the earth for the sake of His servants.

His words ﴿and has completed His favours upon you, outward﴾ refer to the soundness of the bodily limbs, ﴿and inward﴾ refers to the faculties within them. For the limb is outwardly visible, and within it there is an inner power. Do you not see that the eye and the ear are outwardly fat and cartilage, and the tongue and the nose are outwardly flesh and bone, yet in each there is an inner meaning: sight, hearing, taste and smell? The same applies to every limb. The faculty may cease while the limb remains standing. This is better than what has been said, for on this reading the argument is from the favours of the horizons (al-afaq) and the favours of the selves (al-anfus). Thus His words ﴿whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ refer to the favours of the horizons, and His words ﴿and has completed His favours upon you, outward and inward﴾ refer to the favours of the selves. There are many opinions on these matters, mentioned in all the books of tafsir. It is not far-fetched that what we have mentioned was transmitted as a report (maqul manqul), and even if it was not, it does not cease to be a valid and rationally sound interpretation.

* * *

Then God said: ﴿And among the people is one who disputes about God﴾. That is, since oneness has been established through creation and bestowal of favours, among the people there is one who disputes about God and affirms another, either as a god or as a bestower of favours. ﴿Without knowledge, without guidance, and without an illuminating Book.﴾ These are three levels: the level of knowledge ('ilm), guidance (huda), and the Book (kitab). Knowledge is higher than guidance, and guidance is higher than the Book. Its explanation is that knowledge encompasses things that are clear and evident, known without the guidance of a guide. Then guidance encompasses that which is in a book and that which comes through inspiration (ilham) and revelation (wahy). God said ﴿disputes﴾, that disputant does not do so from clear knowledge, nor from guidance received from a guide, nor from a book. It seems that the first refers to one who has been given knowledge from His presence, as God said: ﴿and taught you what you did not know﴾ [al-Nisa': 113].

The second refers to the level of one who has been guided to the straight path through an intermediary, as God said: ﴿One mighty in power taught him﴾ [al-Najm: 5]. The third refers to the level of one who is guided through two intermediaries. For this reason God said: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim. That is the Book, there is no doubt in it, a guidance for the God-fearing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 1-2], and He said in this surah: ﴿a guidance and a mercy for the good-doers﴾ [Luqman: 3], and He said in the surah of prostration: ﴿And We gave Moses the Book and made it a guidance for the Children of Israel﴾ [al-Isra': 2]. So the Book is guidance for the people of the Prophet (peace be upon him), and the Prophet's guidance is from God, exalted is He, without intermediary, or through the intermediary of the Trustworthy Spirit (Ruh al-Amin). God said, then, that the one who disputes disputes not with a knowledge We gave him from Our presence as unveiling (kashf), nor with a guidance We sent to him as revelation, nor with a Book recited to him as admonition.

Then there is another subtle point in it, namely that He said regarding the Book: ﴿nor with an illuminating Book﴾. This is because among the disputants there are some who dispute from a book, but it is distorted, like the Torah after its distortion. Had He said "nor with a Book", one could have said: "He does not dispute without a book, for some of what they say is in their book." Also, the Magians (al-Majus) and the Christians say duality and trinity on the basis of their book. So He said ﴿nor with an illuminating Book﴾, for that book is dark. Since in the first and second levels He did not allow for distortion and alteration, He did not say "without knowledge and without guidance illuminating", or "true", or anything else.

Then He said, may He be exalted: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Follow what Allah has sent down," they say, "Rather, we will follow what we found our fathers upon." Even though Satan was calling them to the punishment of the Blaze?﴾ ﴿And whoever submits his face to Allah while being a doer of good has grasped the most reliable handhold, and to Allah is the outcome of matters.﴾

Speech is more indicative than action, because an action may be permissible, may be forbidden, and they engaged in it, and it may be obligatory in their belief. Speech is clear in its indication. So if we heard the speech of a speaker saying "Do," and we saw his action indicating the opposite of his speech, the obligation would be to take the speech. Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Even though Satan was calling them to the punishment of the Blaze?﴾ This is an interrogation (istifham) in the manner of amazement and denunciation, meaning: Satan calls them to the punishment, and Allah calls to the reward, and yet they follow Satan. Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And whoever submits his face to Allah while being a doer of good has grasped the most reliable handhold, and to Allah is the outcome of matters.﴾ When He had explained the state of the polytheist and the one who disputes about Allah, He explained the state of the Muslim who submits to the command of Allah. His saying, ﴿whoever submits his face to Allah﴾, is an indication of faith, and His saying, ﴿while being a doer of good﴾, is an indication of righteous deeds. So the verse is in the sense of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ [Saba': 37]. His saying, ﴿has grasped the most reliable handhold﴾, means he has held fast to a rope that has no severance, and by means of it he ascends to the highest stations.

In the verse there are issues (masa'il, points of discussion):

The first issue: Here He said, ﴿whoever submits his face to Allah﴾, and in Surat al-Baqarah He said: ﴿Yes, whoever submits his face to Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 112]. So here He used "ila" (to), and there He used the "lam" (for). Al-Zamakhshari said: The meaning of His saying, ﴿submits his face to Allah﴾, is that he makes himself sound (salim), that is, pure (khalis) for Allah, and "the face" means the self and the essence. The meaning of His saying, ﴿submits his face to Allah﴾, is that he submits his self to Allah, as one submits goods to another, and he did not add to this. It is possible to add to it and say: whoever submits himself for Allah has a higher rank than one who submits to Allah, because "ila" denotes the end-point, while "lam" denotes exclusivity. A speaker says, "I have submitted my face to you," meaning, "I turned toward you," and this indicates non-arrival, because turning toward a thing is before reaching it. But His saying, ﴿I have submitted my face for Allah﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 20], conveys exclusivity, and does not indicate the end-point that denotes the distance and the traversing of it in order to arrive. Having known this, we say: In al-Baqarah, the Jews and the Christians said: ﴿None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians﴾ [al-Baqarah: 111]. So Allah responded to them: ﴿That is their wishful thinking. Say, "Produce your proof."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 111]. Then He clarified the corruption of their statement with His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Yes, whoever submits his face to Allah﴾, meaning: you, although you abandon Allah for the sake of this world, turn away from Him toward falsehood, and exchange His verses for a small price, will enter [the Fire], while whoever is wholly for Allah will not enter it. This statement is false. So He presented to them the one who submits himself to Allah, and there is no doubt that refuting them by the case that is more binding is better. So He presented to them the sincere one whose concern is only Allah, and said: You enter Paradise and this one does not enter it. Then He clarified their lie, and said, "Yes," and clarified that for him there is a degree above Paradise, which is the state of being in His presence (al-'indiyyah), with His saying: ﴿then his reward is with his Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 112]. As for here, He intended the promise to the doer of good of reward and of attaining the high degree. So He promised the one below him, so that the one above him would enter it by the more fitting way, and the promise would be general. This is one of the sublime benefits.

In the verse there are issues (masa'il, points of discussion):

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿then has grasped the most reliable handhold﴾. The most reliable of handholds is the side of Allah, because everything other than Him is perishing and severed, while He is enduring with no cessation. Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿and to Allah is the outcome of matters﴾, meaning: he has grasped a handhold that connects him to Allah, and every thing's outcome is to Him. So when what its outcome is toward Him is attained in the present state, the outcome is in the utmost goodness. This is because whoever knows that the outcome of matters is toward One, and then sends gifts to Him before arriving at Him, finds their benefit when he comes before Him. To this the indication was made by His saying: ﴿And whatever good you send forth for yourselves, you will find it with Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 110].

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 31, verses 27–28:

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if whatever trees are on the earth were pens, and the sea, replenished by seven more seas after it, were ink, the words of God would not be exhausted. Indeed, God is Almighty, Wise.﴾ ﴿Your creation and your resurrection are but as a single soul. Indeed, God is All-Hearing, All-Seeing.﴾

When God, exalted is He, said: ﴿To God belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾, and this might suggest that His dominion is finite, since what is in the heavens and what is on the earth are confined within them, while the clear judgment of reason is that both are finite, He explained that in His power and knowledge there are wonders without end. So He said: ﴿And if whatever trees are on the earth were pens﴾, which are used for writing, and the seas were ink, the wonders of God's creation would not run out. On this basis, the "word" (kalimah) is explained as "wonder" (ajībah). Its justification is that the wonders are by His saying "Be" (kun), and "kun" is a word (kalimah), and naming the cause by the name of the effect is permissible. A warrior says to his opponent in combat, "I am your death," and it is said of a medicine to a patient, "This is your cure." The proof of the soundness of this is that God, exalted is He, named Jesus a "word," because he was a marvelous matter and a strange creation, in that he came into existence without a father.

If someone says: the verse was revealed concerning the Jews, when they said: "God has mentioned everything in the Torah, and nothing has been left out that He has not mentioned." So He said: what is in the Torah, in relation to the speech of God, is nothing but a drop from the seas. And He revealed this verse.

It is also said: it was revealed concerning a man who said to the Prophet, peace be upon him: "You say: ﴿And you have been given of knowledge only a little﴾ [al-Isra: 85], and you say: ﴿And whoever is given wisdom has certainly been given much good﴾ [al-Baqarah: 269]." So the verse was revealed indicating that it is abundant good in relation to the servants, and in relation to God and His knowledge it is little. It is also said: it was revealed in refutation of the disbelievers, when they said that what Muhammad brings will come to an end, so He said: it is the speech of God, and it does not end.

What has been mentioned of the occasions of revelation contradicts what you have mentioned of the exegesis, because they indicate that what is meant is speech. We say: the differing of the statements you have mentioned concerning it indicates the permissibility of what we have mentioned, because if it is suitable as an answer to these different things that you have mentioned, it is known that it is general. What we have mentioned does not contradict this, because the speech of God is wondrous, inimitable, and no one can bring the like of it. When we say that the wonders of God have no end, His speech enters into them. It cannot be said: you have made the speech created; because we say: what is created is the letter and the composition, and it is wondrous; as for the words, they are among the attributes of God, exalted is He.

Know that the verse, although it was revealed in an order other than the one in which it is written, the written order in which the Qur'an is arranged is by the command of God, for it was written thus by the command of the Messenger, and the command of the Messenger is from the command of God, and this is established and certain from the traditions of the arrangement that is in it. Then the verse contains subtleties.

The first: He said: ﴿And if whatever trees are on the earth were pens﴾. He made "tree" singular and "pens" plural, and He did not say "And if what is on the earth of trees were pens," nor did He say "And if what is on the earth of a tree were a pen," as an indication of abundance, meaning: even if there were pens for every single tree.

The second: His saying ﴿and the sea, replenished﴾: the definiteness of "the sea" (al-bahr) with the article is for the generalization of the genus, and every sea is ink. Then His saying ﴿replenished by seven more seas after it﴾ is an indication of seas that do not exist, meaning: if the existing seas were replenished by seven other seas. His saying ﴿seven﴾ does not mean that they are restricted to seven; rather the indication is to increase and abundance, even if by a thousand seas. The seven was singled out for mention from among the numbers because it is a large number which in custom encompasses the countable things. And what indicates this are several aspects:

The first: what is known to everyone because of their need for it is time and place, because place contains bodies and time contains actions. But place is limited to seven climes, and time to seven days; and because the wandering planets are seven, and the astrologers attributed matters to them, so seven became like a number that encompasses the multitudes that occur in custom, and it was used for every large number.

The second: units up to ten are the first decade, and what comes after it begins again from the units, so one says eleven, twelve; then hundreds from tens, and thousands from hundreds. Once this is known, we say: the least number from which most countable things are formed is three, because it needs two extremes: a beginning, an end, and a middle. For this reason it is said: the least that a noun or a verb can be is three letters. So when three is the first part of the ten, which is the original number, seven remains as the larger part. When the purpose is to show abundance, seven is mentioned. For this reason, the countable items in acts of worship, such as the glorifications in the transitions within the prayers, are three, and the repetitions in ablution are three, to ease the matter for the one obligated, by being content with the first part.

Having established this, we say: his saying, peace be upon him: "The believer eats in one intestine, and the disbeliever eats in seven intestines" is an indication of the smallness and largeness of eating, without intending seven specifically. It may be said that hell has seven gates by this interpretation; then on this basis our saying that paradise has eight gates is an indication of its increase, for in it is the best reward and more, so it has many gates, more than the abundance of others. What indicates what we have mentioned regarding seven is that the Arabs, at the eighth, add a waw; al-Farra' says it is the "waw of eight," and that is only for beginning anew, because the number is complete in custom with seven, and then with the eighth there is a fresh beginning.

The third subtlety: He did not say "the replenishment" concerning the pens, for two reasons.

One of them: His saying ﴿And if whatever trees are on the earth were pens﴾: we have explained that what is meant is that for the number of every existing tree there be pens, so the pens would be more than the existing trees; and His saying concerning the sea ﴿and the sea, replenished by seven more seas after it﴾ is an indication that if the sea were more than what exists, the pen and the sea would be equal in meaning.

The second: the deficiency by writing affects the ink more, for it is what is exhausted, while a single pen can be used to write many books; so He mentioned replenishment for the sea, which is like the ink.

* * *

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, God is Almighty, Wise.﴾ When He mentioned that His dominion is vast, He pointed to what confirms that, saying: ﴿Indeed, God is Almighty, Wise﴾, that is, of perfect power, so He has objects of power without end; otherwise power would end at a point where it is not fit for bringing into existence. And He is Wise, of perfect knowledge, so in His knowledge there is what has no end, and it is established that if the sea were ink, what is in His knowledge and power would not be exhausted.

* * *

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Your creation and your resurrection are but as a single soul.﴾ When He explained the perfection of His power and knowledge, He mentioned what nullifies their deeming resurrection far-fetched, and said: ﴿Your creation and your resurrection are but as a single soul﴾, for whoever has no end to His words says to the dead, "Be," and they are.

* * *

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, God is All-Hearing, All-Seeing.﴾ All-Hearing of what they say, All-Seeing of what they do. So His being capable of resurrection and encompassing words and deeds necessitates complete avoidance and perfect caution.

Then His saying ﴿replenished by seven more seas after it﴾ is an indication of seas that do not exist, meaning: if the existing seas were replenished by seven other seas. His saying ﴿seven﴾ does not mean that they are restricted to seven; rather the indication is to increase and abundance, even if by a thousand seas. The seven was singled out for mention from among the numbers because it is a large number which in custom encompasses the countable things. And what indicates this are several aspects:

The first: what is known to everyone because of their need for it is time and place, because place contains bodies and time contains actions. But place is limited to seven climes, and time to seven days; and because the wandering planets are seven, and the astrologers attributed matters to them, so seven became like a number that encompasses the multitudes that occur in custom, and it was used for every large number.

The second: units up to ten are the first decade, and what comes after it begins again from the units, so one says eleven, twelve; then hundreds from tens, and thousands from hundreds. Once this is known, we say: the least number from which most countable things are formed is three, because it needs two extremes: a beginning, an end, and a middle. For this reason it is said: the least that a noun or a verb can be is three letters. So when three is the first part of the ten, which is the original number, seven remains as the larger part. When the purpose is to show abundance, seven is mentioned. For this reason, the countable items in acts of worship, such as the glorifications in the transitions within the prayers, are three, and the repetitions in ablution are three, to ease the matter for the one obligated, by being content with the first part.

Having established this, we say: his saying, peace be upon him: "The believer eats in one intestine, and the disbeliever eats in seven intestines" is an indication of the smallness and largeness of eating, without intending seven specifically. It may be said that hell has seven gates by this interpretation; then on this basis our saying that paradise has eight gates is an indication of its increase, for in it is the best reward and more, so it has many gates, more than the abundance of others. What indicates what we have mentioned regarding seven is that the Arabs, at the eighth, add a waw; al-Farra' says it is the "waw of eight," and that is only for beginning anew, because the number is complete in custom with seven, and then with the eighth there is a fresh beginning.

The third subtlety: He did not say "the replenishment" concerning the pens, for two reasons.

One of them: His saying ﴿And if whatever trees are on the earth were pens﴾: we have explained that what is meant is that for the number of every existing tree there be pens, so the pens would be more than the existing trees; and His saying concerning the sea ﴿and the sea, replenished by seven more seas after it﴾ is an indication that if the sea were more than what exists, the pen and the sea would be equal in meaning.

The second: the deficiency by writing affects the ink more, for it is what is exhausted, while a single pen can be used to write many books; so He mentioned replenishment for the sea, which is like the ink.

* * *

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, God is Almighty, Wise.﴾ When He mentioned that His dominion is vast, He pointed to what confirms that, saying: ﴿Indeed, God is Almighty, Wise﴾, that is, of perfect power, so He has objects of power without end; otherwise power would end at a point where it is not fit for bringing into existence. And He is Wise, of perfect knowledge, so in His knowledge there is what has no end, and it is established that if the sea were ink, what is in His knowledge and power would not be exhausted.

* * *

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Your creation and your resurrection are but as a single soul.﴾ When He explained the perfection of His power and knowledge, He mentioned what nullifies their deeming resurrection far-fetched, and said: ﴿Your creation and your resurrection are but as a single soul﴾, for whoever has no end to His words says to the dead, "Be," and they are.

* * *

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, God is All-Hearing, All-Seeing.﴾ All-Hearing of what they say, All-Seeing of what they do. So His being capable of resurrection and encompassing words and deeds necessitates complete avoidance and perfect caution.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 31, verse 29:

Then the Exalted said: ﴿Have you not seen that Allah causes the night to enter into the day and causes the day to enter into the night, and has subjected the sun and the moon, each running to a specified term, and that Allah is Acquainted with what you do?﴾

It may be said that the reason for this order is that when Allah, the Exalted, said, ﴿Have you not seen that Allah has subjected to you what is in the heavens and what is in the earth?﴾ in general terms, He then mentioned some of what is in them in particular terms: ﴿He causes the night to enter into the day﴾. His saying ﴿and has subjected the sun and the moon﴾ is a reference to what is in the heavens. His saying after this, ﴿Have you not seen that the ships run through the sea by the favor of Allah?﴾ (Luqman 31:31), is a reference to what is in the earth. It may also be said that the reason is this: when Allah, the Exalted, mentioned the resurrection, some people said, ﴿Nothing destroys us except time﴾ (al-Jathiyah 45:24), and time is the nights and days. Allah, the Exalted, said: these nights and days to which you attribute death and life are by the power of Allah, the Exalted. So He said: ﴿Have you not seen that Allah causes the night to enter into the day and causes the day to enter into the night?﴾

Now, if someone were to say: this is a regulated alternation. Sometimes the sun's arc above the earth is greater than its arc below the earth, so the night is shorter and the day longer; at other times it is the reverse; and at other times they are equal. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿and has subjected the sun and the moon﴾, meaning: if you do not acknowledge that all these things originally come from Allah, then you must acknowledge that they all return to Allah, the Exalted. The terms are by the measure (al-madad), and the measure is by the movement of the stars; the movement of the stars is only by Allah and His power. There are several issues in the verse:

The first issue: the phrase ﴿causes the night to enter into the day﴾ admits of two meanings.

One of them: it is said that what is meant is the entering of the night into the time of the day, that is, He makes the night exist in the time in which there was day. This is because if the night is, for example, twelve hours and then it lengthens, the night comes to exist in a time in which there was day.

The second: it is said that what is meant is the entering of the duration of the night into the day, that is, He makes the duration of the night enter the day. This is because if the night is, as we have mentioned, twelve hours, and then it shortens, the duration of the night comes to exist in the day. This cannot be otherwise, because the entering of the night into the day is impossible to exist, so what we have mentioned of an implied ellipsis is necessary. But the first is preferable, because night and day are actions, and actions are in times, since time is a container. So our saying "the night in the time of the day" is closer than our saying "the time of the night in the day", because the second makes the container into the contained.

Having established this, we say: the saying of the Exalted, ﴿causes the night to enter into the day﴾, means: He brings it into existence at a time in which there was day. Allah, the Exalted, put the bringing into existence of the night before the bringing into existence of the day in many places, as in His saying, ﴿and We made the night and the day two signs﴾ (al-Isra 17:12), His saying, ﴿and made the darkness and the light﴾ (al-An'am 6:1), and His saying, ﴿and the alternation of the night and the day﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:164). Of the same kind is His saying, ﴿He created death and life that He may test you as to which of you is best in deed﴾ (al-Mulk 67:2). This is a reference to a judgmental issue: darkness may be thought to be the absence of light, the night the absence of day, and life the absence of death. This is not so, for in the pre-eternity (al-azal) there was no day, no light, and no life for a possible thing, and it cannot be said that there was in it death, darkness, or night. These matters are like blindness and deafness. Blindness and deafness are not merely the absence of sight and the absence of hearing, since a stone and a tree have no sight and no hearing, and neither of them is called deaf or blind.

Having known this, we say: that in which blindness and deafness are realized must necessarily have an inclination toward their opposites, otherwise it would not be called blind or deaf. What has an inclination toward something and whose inclination follows its course does not make the soul seek a cause for it; for whoever sees a man earning a living in the market does not ask why he entered the market. But what stands contrary to the expected course makes the soul seek a cause for it, as when someone sees a king in the market and asks why he entered. So the cause of blindness and deafness is sought by everyone, who says, "Why did so-and-so become blind?" and does not say, "Why did so-and-so become sighted?" Since this is so, Allah, the Exalted, put first what the soul seeks the cause of, namely the night, which is on the same footing as blindness, darkness, and death, because each of these is sought for its cause. Then He mentioned the other matter after it.

The second issue: He said ﴿causes﴾ in the present tense (yūliju), and He said ﴿has subjected﴾ (sakhkhara) in the past tense concerning the sun and the moon. This is because the entering of the night into the day is a matter that renews itself every season, indeed every day, whereas the subjecting of the sun and the moon is a continuous matter, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿until it returned like an old date-stalk﴾ (Ya-Sin 36:39).

The third issue: He put the sun before the moon, although the night, in which the moon has authority, precedes the day, in which the sun has authority. This is for what we have explained: the precedence of the night was because the souls seek its cause more than they seek the cause of the day. Here too it is so, because the sun, being greater and more magnificent, is more wondrous, and the soul seeks the cause of a wondrous matter more than it seeks the cause of a matter that is not wondrous.

The fourth issue: what is the connection of His saying, ﴿and that Allah is Acquainted with what you do﴾, to what precedes it? We say: since night and day are the place of actions, He made clear that what occurs in these two times, which are under the disposal of Allah, is not hidden from Allah.

The fifth issue: His saying, ﴿Have you not seen﴾, admits of two meanings.

One of them: the address is to the Prophet ﷺ. This is the view of most scholars. It is as though He left addressing others, because as for those who are disbelievers, there is no benefit in addressing them given their obstinacy, and as for those who are believers, they are already following the command of the Prophet, peace be upon him, and looking to him.

The second meaning: it is said that what is meant is admonition (al-wa'z), and the admonisher addresses without naming anyone, saying to a great gathering, "O poor one, to Allah is your return; who then is your helper, and why is your negligence?" So His saying, ﴿Have you not seen﴾, is an address of this kind, meaning: O heedless one, have you not seen this clear matter?

[Page 140]

That is the truth, because Allah is the Truth, and what they call upon besides Him is falsehood, and Allah is the Most High, the Great. ﴿That is because Allah is the Truth, and what they call upon besides Him is falsehood, and Allah is the Most High, the Great.﴾

When the Exalted mentioned the attributes of perfection in His saying, ﴿Indeed, Allah is the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy﴾, and His saying, ﴿Indeed, Allah is Almighty, All-Wise﴾, and His saying, ﴿Indeed, Allah is All-Hearing, All-Seeing﴾, and He alluded to will and perfection in His saying, ﴿The words of Allah would not be exhausted﴾, and in His saying, ﴿He causes the night to enter into the day﴾, and in summary, His saying, ﴿He is the Self-Sufficient﴾ is an allusion to every negative attribute. For whoever is self-sufficient cannot be an accident needing a substance to subsist, nor a body needing a place to persist, nor one of the contingent beings needing a bringer-into-existence. Then He mentioned, after this, all the affirmative attributes, explicitly and implicitly, since life is included within knowledge and power. He said, ﴿That is because Allah is the Truth﴾, meaning that this attribution, that He is the Truth, [is what is affirmed]. Al-Haqq (the Truth) means existence and permanence, and the one who is Truth is Allah. He is the absolutely enduring, who has no cessation, and this is existence. For the correct position is that His existence is not other than His essence. Everything other than Him is therefore liable to cessation when considered in itself, while Allah has existence and permanence when considered in Himself. So He is the Truth, and whatever is other than Him is falsehood, because al-Batil (falsehood) is that which ceases. It is said: "Its shadow was annulled (baṭala) when it ceased." And since He has permanence from every aspect, He is perfect with no deficiency in Him.

Then know that the philosophers (al-hukama', the wise) said: Allah is complete (tamm) and beyond completeness (fawq al-tamm). They divided beings into four categories: deficient (naqis), sufficient (muktafi), complete (tamm), and beyond completeness (fawq al-tamm). The deficient is that which does not have what it should have, such as the child, the sick person, and the blind person. The sufficient is the one given what enables him to meet his need at its time, such as the human being and the animal, who have the instruments by which they meet their needs at their times, but these are subject to dissolution and cessation. The complete is the one who has acquired everything that is permissible for him, even if he does not need it, such as the angels brought near, who have degrees that are not increased or diminished, and Allah does not take anything from them, as "Jibril, upon him peace, said: 'If I came near by a fingertip, I would be burned.'" This is in accordance with His saying, ﴿There is none of us but has a known station﴾ [al-Saffat: 164].

Beyond completeness is the one who has acquired what is permissible for him, while for everything else what is permissible for it or what it needs has been acquired. But Allah, the Exalted, has acquired for Himself every attribute of perfection and qualities of majesty that are permissible for Him, so He is complete. Whereas for others, everything that is permissible for them or that they need has been acquired, so He is beyond completeness.

Having established this, we say: His saying, ﴿He is the Truth﴾, is an allusion to completeness. His saying, ﴿and that Allah is the Most High, the Great﴾ means beyond completeness. His saying, ﴿the Most High﴾, means in His attributes, and His saying, ﴿the Great﴾, means in His essence. This negates that He would be a body in a place, for then He would be a body measured by a measure, so something greater than Him could be supposed, and He would be small in relation to what is supposed. Rather, He is Great absolutely, greater than everything that can be conceived.

[Page 141]

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Have you not seen that the ships sail through the sea by the favor of Allah, that He may show you of His signs? Indeed in that are signs for every steadfast, grateful person.﴾

When He mentioned a heavenly sign with His words ﴿Have you not seen that Allah causes the night to enter into the day and causes the day to enter into the night, and has subjected the sun and the moon?﴾, and alluded to the cause and the effect, He mentioned an earthly sign, and alluded to the cause and the effect. So His words ﴿the ships sail﴾ are an allusion to the effect (al-musabbab), and His words ﴿by the favor of Allah﴾ are an allusion to the cause (al-sabab), that is, to the wind, which is by the command of Allah. ﴿That He may show you of His signs﴾ means: He shows you, by making them run by His favor, ﴿of His signs﴾, that is, some of His signs. Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed in that are signs for every steadfast, grateful person.﴾ (ṣabbār) is one who is steadfast in hardship, (shakūr) is one who is grateful in ease. That is because the believer is mindful in times of hardship and tribulation, and mindful in times of blessings and bounties; so he is patient when a calamity befalls him, and thankful when a blessing comes to him. It has been related in the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Faith is of two halves: half is patience, and half is gratitude." This is an indication that the obligations (al-takālīf) are acts and abstentions (turūk), and abstentions are patience from what is habitual, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Fasting is patience, and acts are gratitude for what is good."

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And when a wave covers them like shadows, they call upon God, sincere to Him in religion. But when He delivers them to the land, some of them are moderate. And none rejects Our signs except every treacherous ungrateful one.﴾

When God mentioned that in that there are signs (ayat), He mentioned that all of them acknowledge it, except that the perceptive person recognizes it first, while one whose sight is weak does not recognize it first. So when a wave covers him and he falls into hardship, he acknowledges that everything is from God, and he calls upon Him sincerely, meaning he leaves aside everyone other than Him and forgets all who are besides Him. Then when He delivers him from that hardship, some remain in that state, and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿some of them are moderate﴾. And some return to polytheism (shirk), and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿And none rejects Our signs except every treacherous ungrateful one.﴾ There are several issues in this verse:

The first issue: His saying ﴿a wave like shadows﴾. He used the singular for "wave" (mawj) and the plural for "shadows" (zulal). It has been said that its meaning is "like mountains," and it has been said "like clouds," indicating the greatness of the wave. It may be said that a single great wave shows a rising and a falling in it, and if you look at a single stream of a great river, this becomes clear to you, so it is like closely joined mountains.

The second issue: In al-Ankabut (He said), ﴿So when they board the ship, they call upon God﴾ [al-Ankabut: 65], then He said: ﴿But when He delivers them to the land, behold, they associate partners [with Him]﴾. And here He said: ﴿But when He delivers them to the land, some of them are moderate﴾. We say: Since He mentioned here a great matter, namely the wave like mountains, the effect of that remained in their hearts, so some of them emerged as moderate, i.e., in disbelief, and that is the one who was restrained to some degree, or moderate in sincerity, so some of it remained with him and he did not remain in the state of sincerity he had been in. Whereas there, He did not mention with boarding the sea a witnessing of such a matter, so He mentioned their associating partners, since no trace of it remained with them.

The third issue: His saying ﴿And none rejects Our signs﴾ is in contrast to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed in that are signs﴾. It means: the patient (sabbar) and grateful (shakur) one acknowledges them, while the treacherous (khattar) and ungrateful (kafur) one rejects them. The word "sabbar" is paired with "khattar" in form and meaning, and "kafur" is paired with "shakur." As for the form, it is evident. As for the meaning, the khattar is the one who is extremely treacherous or intensely treacherous, and treachery arises only from lack of patience, because the patient person, if he does not make a covenant with anyone from whom harm is not expected, then he is patient and entrusts the matter to God; but the treacherous one makes a covenant and is not patient in keeping the covenant, so he breaks it. As for "kafur" being in contrast to "shakur" in meaning, it is evident.

Then God Most High said: "O mankind, fear your Lord and dread a Day when no parent will avail anything for his child, nor will a child avail anything for his parent. Indeed, the promise of God is true, so let not the worldly life deceive you, nor let the Deceiver deceive you concerning God."

Page 143

When he had mentioned the proofs from the beginning of the surah to its end, he exhorted them to piety (taqwa). Because He, Exalted is He, is One, He made the complete taqwa obligatory. For whoever knows that the affair is in the hands of two does not fear one of them as much as he would fear if the affair were in the hand of only one of them. Then He reinforced the fear by mentioning the Day on which God will judge among the servants. This is because a king who is one, and of whom it is known that he does not know anything and does not review his subjects, is not feared as much as one who is known to have a day of review and investigation. Then He reinforced it with His saying: "No parent will avail anything for his child," because a criminal who knows that he has with the king someone who will speak on his behalf and settle what is due against him with a ransom from his earnings does not fear as much as one who knows that he has no one to settle for him what is due against him. Then He mentioned two persons in the utmost compassion and love, namely the parent and the child, so that one may infer the higher from the lower. Mentioning both the child and the parent together contains a subtle point: among matters, the father hastens to bear on behalf of the child, such as paying money and bearing pains, while the child does not hasten to bear for the parent as the parent hastens to bear for the child. And among them are matters in which the child hastens to bear on behalf of the parent while the parent does not hasten to bear on behalf of the child, such as humiliation. For whoever wants to bring the father of someone before a governor or judge, it is easy for the son to avert the humiliation from his father and to appear himself in his place. But when the matter reaches the point of pain, it is easy for the father to avert the pain from his son and to bear it himself. So His saying "no parent will avail anything for his child" concerns averting pains, and "nor will a child avail anything for his parent" concerns averting humiliation. And in His saying "will avail" (lā yajzī) [there is a further point].

His saying "nor will a child avail" (wa-lā mawlūdun huwa jāzin) is another subtle point: we have mentioned that an act may be attributed to one for whom it is not fitting and not part of his nature. For when a king sews something, one says "he sews" but one does not say "he is a tailor." Likewise, one who weaves something that is not his profession is said to "weave" but is not called "a weaver." Knowing this, we say: it is part of the child's nature to be one who avails for his parent, because of the rights he has over him, while the parent avails out of compassion, and it is not obligatory upon him. Therefore He said of the parent "does not avail," and of the child "nor is a child one who avails."

* * *

Then He said, Exalted is He: "Indeed, the promise of God is true." This admits of two meanings.

The first: that it is a confirmation of the Day, meaning: fear a Day of this description, which will certainly come, for God has promised it, and His promise is true.

The second: that it is a confirmation of the non-avail, meaning: "no parent will avail for his child," because God promised: "No bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another" [al-An'am: 164], and the promise of God is true, so there will be no avail. The first is better and clearer.

* * *

Then He said, Exalted is He: "So let not the worldly life deceive you." That is: if the matter is so, then do not be deluded by the world, for it is passing, given the occurrence of that mentioned Day by the true promise.

* * *

Then He said, Exalted is He: "Nor let the Deceiver deceive you concerning God." That is: the world should not deceive you by itself, nor should you be deluded by it, even if a deceiver from a commanding self (nafs ammārah) or a devil leads you to love it. People are of divisions: among them is one whom the world calls to itself so that he inclines to it; and among them is one whom Satan whispers into his breast and whom he adorns the world in his eyes, promising him and saying: "You will obtain the Hereafter through it, or you will enjoy it, and then you will repent, so that the world and the Hereafter will both be gathered for you." So He forbade them both matters, and said: Be a third division: those who do not turn toward the world nor toward whoever beautifies the world in the eyes.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 31, verse 34:

Page 144
Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, Allah has knowledge of the Hour, and He sends down the rain, and He knows what is in the wombs. And no soul knows what it will earn tomorrow, and no soul knows in what land it will die. Indeed, Allah is Knowing and Acquainted.﴾
Some of the exegetes (mufassirun) say: Allah, exalted is He, by this verse negated the knowledge of five matters from anyone other than Him, and that is so; but the intended meaning is not that. For Allah knows the single atom (jawhar fard) that was in a heap of sand at the time of the Flood, and how many times the wind carried it from east to west, and He knows where it is while no one else knows it. And because He knows that after these years there will exist a particle in a wilderness that no one traverses and no one knows but Him. So there is no point in singling out these things for mention. Rather, the truth in this matter is that we say: when Allah said, ﴿Fear a Day when no father will avail his son at all﴾ and mentioned that it is certain to occur by His saying, ﴿Indeed, the promise of Allah is true﴾, it was as if a questioner asked: "When will this Day be?" So it was answered that this knowledge is among what has not been granted to anyone other than Allah, but it is certain to occur. Then He mentioned the two proofs we have mentioned repeatedly for resurrection. One of them: the revival of the earth after its death, as He said: ﴿And indeed, they had been, before it was sent down upon them, before that, despairing﴾ ﴿So look at the effects of the mercy of Allah – how He gives life to the earth after its death. Indeed, that [same One] will surely give life to the dead﴾ [al-Rum: 50]. And He said: ﴿And He brings to life the earth after its death; and thus you will be brought forth﴾. And here He said: "O questioner, you do not know its time, but it is certain to occur, and Allah is capable of it just as He is capable of reviving the earth," as He said: ﴿And it is He who sends down the rain﴾ and He said: ﴿He revives the earth﴾.

The second of them: creation at the beginning, as He said: ﴿And it is He who begins creation and then repeats it﴾ [al-Rum: 27] and Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: Travel through the earth and observe how He began creation; then Allah will produce the final creation﴾ [al-Ankabut: 20], and so on besides that. Here He said, ﴿and He knows what is in the wombs,﴾ as an indication that the Hour, although you do not know it, is certain to occur, and Allah is capable of it; and just as He is capable of creating within the wombs, so He is capable of creating from the bones. Then He said to that seeker of knowledge: "O questioner, you ask about the Hour, when its arrival will be. But there are matters more important than it that you do not know. You do not know your livelihood and your return. You do not know what you will earn tomorrow, although it is your act and your time. You do not know where you will die, although it is your concern and your place. So how would you know when the Hour will come? Allah has not informed you of what you will earn tomorrow, although in it are benefits upon which your affairs of this day are built. Nor did He inform you where you will die, although in it are purposes by which you would prepare your affairs through that knowledge. He did not inform you so that, at a time concerning sustenance, you would turn back to Allah, exalted is He, relying upon Allah. Nor did He inform you of the land in which you will die, lest you feel secure from death while you are in another land. So if He has not informed you of what you need, how would He inform you of what you have no need for, namely the Hour?! What you need is knowledge that it will occur, and you have been informed of that from Allah through the tongues of His prophets."

* * *
Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing and Acquainted.﴾ When He first restricted His knowledge to the things mentioned, by His saying, ﴿Indeed, Allah has knowledge of the Hour,﴾ He mentioned that His knowledge is not restricted to them, but He is Knowing absolutely of everything. His knowledge is not merely of the outward aspects of things; rather, He is Acquainted (Khabir), His knowledge reaching the inner realities of things. And Allah knows best what is correct.
